function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends an HTTP GET request to retrieve Device Connector Versions information from a specified URL. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: The URL to which the GET request is sent. The URL points to a JSON file containing Device Connector Versions information.

params.description: Optional query parameters to include in the GET request as key-value pairs.

message.content:
Below is a “tool‑kit” of ways to pull **detailed information** about a network interface on a Linux host.  
Pick the method that best fits your environment (CLI, SNMP, REST API, etc.) and the level of detail you need.

---

## 1. Quick CLI snapshot

| Command | What it shows | Typical output snippet |
|---------|---------------|------------------------|
| `ip link show <iface>` | Interface state, MAC, MTU, flags | `2: eth0: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 1500 qdisc pfifo_fast state UP mode DEFAULT group default qlen 1000` |
| `ip addr show <iface>` | IP addresses, netmask, broadcast | `inet 192.168.1.10/24 brd 192.168.1.255 scope global eth0` |
| `ip -s link show <iface>` | Packet counters (rx/tx) | `RX:  12345 packets,  67890 bytes` |
| `ip -d link show <iface>` | Driver, hardware info, link speed | `link/ether 00:11:22:33:44:55 brd ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff` |
| `ethtool <iface>` | Driver, firmware, speed, duplex, autoneg | `Speed: 1000Mb/s  Duplex: Full  Port: Twisted Pair` |
| `ethtool -S <iface>` | Raw statistics counters | `rx_packets: 12345  tx_packets: 67890` |
| `ethtool -i <iface>` | Driver name & version | `driver: e1000e  version: 3.2.6-k` |
| `ethtool -d <iface>` | Driver diagnostics (if supported) | `Driver diagnostics: ...` |
| `ethtool -k <iface>` | Feature flags (e.g., tx‑offload) | `tx-checksumming: on  tx-vlan-offload: off` |

> **Tip:**  
> `ip -details link show <iface>` (or `ip -d link show <iface>`) gives a more verbose dump that includes driver, firmware, and link‑layer details.

---

## 2. Inspecting `/sys/class/net`

The `/sys` filesystem exposes low‑level attributes:

```bash
# Basic attributes
cat /sys/class/net/<iface>/address          # MAC
cat /sys/class/net/<iface>/mtu              # MTU
cat /sys/class/net/<iface>/operstate        # up/down
cat /sys/class/net/<iface>/flags            # bitmask of flags

# Driver & hardware
cat /sys/class/net/<iface>/driver/name      # driver name
cat /sys/class/net/<iface>/device/vendor    # PCI vendor ID
cat /sys/class/net/<iface>/device/device    # PCI device ID
cat /sys/class/net/<iface>/device/modalias  # modalias string

# Statistics
cat /sys/class/net/<iface>/statistics/rx_bytes
cat /sys/class/net/<iface>/statistics/tx_bytes
```

> **Why use `/sys`?**  
> It’s the canonical source for kernel‑reported values and works even when `ethtool` isn’t installed.

---

## 3. Using NetworkManager (if present)

```bash
nmcli device show <iface>
```

Sample output:

```
GENERAL.DEVICE:                         eth0
GENERAL.TYPE:                           ethernet
GENERAL.HWADDR:                         00:11:22:33:44:55
IP4.ADDRESS[1]:                         192.168.1.10/24
IP4.GATEWAY:                            192.168.1.1
IP4.DNS[1]:                             8.8.8.8
```

> **When to use?**  
> If your system relies on NetworkManager, this gives you the *logical* view (DHCP, VPN, etc.) in addition to the raw hardware data.

---

## 4. SNMP (for remote devices)

```bash
snmpwalk -v2c -c public <host> IF-MIB::ifTable
```

Key OIDs:

| OID | Meaning |
|-----|---------|
| `ifDescr` | Interface name |
| `ifType` | Interface type (ethernetCsmacd = 6) |
| `ifMtu` | MTU |
| `ifSpeed` | Speed (bits/sec) |
| `ifPhysAddress` | MAC |
| `ifOperStatus` | Operational status (up/down) |
| `ifInOctets` / `ifOutOctets` | Traffic counters |

> **Note:**  
> SNMP requires the agent to be enabled and the community string (`public` in the example) to be correct.

---

## 5. REST API / Device Connector (if you’re on a managed platform)

If your environment exposes a REST endpoint for device connectors (e.g., Cisco DNA Center, Juniper Contrail, etc.), you can query the interface details via a GET request:

```http
GET https://api.example.com/v1/interfaces/<iface-id>
Authorization: Bearer <token>
```

Typical JSON response:

```json
{
  "id": "eth0",
  "mac": "00:11:22:33:44:55",
  "mtu": 1500,
  "speed": "1000Mbps",
  "duplex": "full",
  "state": "up",
  "statistics": {
    "rx_bytes": 12345678,
    "tx_bytes": 87654321
  }
}
```

> **How to call it programmatically**  
> Use `curl`, `requests` (Python), or any HTTP client.  
> Example with `curl`:

```bash
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
     https://api.example.com/v1/interfaces/eth0
```

---

## 6. Putting it all together – a one‑liner

```bash
# Show driver, firmware, speed, MAC, IP, and traffic stats in one go
ip -d link show eth0 | grep -E 'link/ether|state|driver|firmware|speed|duplex' && \
ip addr show eth0 | grep inet && \
ethtool -S eth0 | head -n 10
```

---

## 7. Common pitfalls & troubleshooting

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---------|--------------|-----|
| `ethtool: No such device` | Interface name typo or not present | Verify with `ip link` |
| `Permission denied` | Need root | Run with `sudo` or as root |
| `SNMP timeout` | Agent disabled or firewall blocking | Enable SNMP agent, open port 161 |
| `Interface shows “down” but traffic is flowing` | Virtual interface or bridge | Check `brctl show` or `ip link show` for bridge members |
| `Speed shows “unknown”` | Driver doesn’t expose speed | Use `ethtool -i` to check driver support |

---

### Bottom line

- **For local, quick checks**: `ip`, `ethtool`, and `/sys` are your best friends.
- **For remote or managed devices**: SNMP or a REST API is the way to go.
- **For a full picture** (driver, firmware, stats, logical config): combine the above tools.

Feel free to let me know which environment you’re working in (bare‑metal, virtual machine, container, managed network device, etc.) and I can tailor the commands even further!
